expectedText:
BACKGROUND CHECK DISCLOSURE & AUTHORIZATION
Prepared for Jordan Lee · Acme, Inc.

DISCLOSURE
Acme, Inc. may obtain a consumer report about Jordan Lee for employment purposes — a report from a background-check company that can cover things like credit history, criminal records, and past employment or education. This document is, on purpose, only this disclosure. For most applicants, federal law requires that disclosure to appear in a document that consists solely of the disclosure — nothing else added in, not a liability waiver, not other contract terms.

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "a clear and conspicuous disclosure has been made in writing to the consumer at any time before the report is procured or caused to be procured, in a document that consists solely of the disclosure, that a consumer report may be obtained for employment purposes"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(2)(A)(i) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, stand-alone disclosure requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681b)
  "We hold that a prospective employer violates Section 1681b(b)(2)(A) when it procures a job applicant’s consumer report after including a liability waiver in the same document as the statutorily mandated disclosure. We also hold that, in light of the clear statutory language that the disclosure document must consist “solely” of the disclosure, a prospective employer’s violation of the FCRA is “willful” when the employer includes terms in addition to the disclosure, such as the liability waiver here, before procuring a consumer report or causing one to be procured."
  — Syed v. M-I, LLC, 853 F.3d 492 (9th Cir. 2017) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4340133/sarmad-syed-v-m-i-llc/)
  "If a consumer described in subparagraph (C) applies for employment by mail, telephone, computer, or other similar means, at any time before a consumer report is procured or caused to be procured in connection with that application— (i) the person who procures the consumer report on the consumer for employment purposes shall provide to the consumer, by oral, written, or electronic means, notice that a consumer report may be obtained for employment purposes"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(2)(B)-(C) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, the transportation-applicant exception to the stand-alone-document rule (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681b)
  Known gap: A federal appeals court has already held that adding other terms to this same document — the case involved a liability waiver — isn't just a technical overreach; it's a violation of this specific requirement, and a knowing one counts as "willful" under the statute, which exposes the employer to statutory and punitive damages beyond whatever actual harm resulted. There's a narrow statutory exception to the stand-alone-document rule itself: an applicant for a position the Secretary of Transportation regulates, or one subject to state transportation-agency safety regulation, who applies by mail, phone, computer, or similar means can instead be given oral, written, or electronic notice — no stand-alone document required for that specific applicant class. Separately, this covers the federal floor only. A number of states add their own background-check disclosure, timing, or "ban the box" requirements on top of this, and this document doesn't catalog them.

AUTHORIZATION
By signing below, Jordan Lee authorizes Acme, Inc. to procure the consumer report described above. Federal law allows this authorization to appear on the same document as the disclosure — that's one deliberate exception to the stand-alone-document rule, written into the statute itself (a separate, narrower exception also exists for certain transportation-industry applicants, covered in the Disclosure clause's own gap).

[Verified — checked 2026-09-01]
  "the consumer has authorized in writing (which authorization may be made on the document referred to in clause (i)) the procurement of the report by that person"
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(2)(A)(ii) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, written authorization requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681b)
  "Congress amended the statute in 1998 to add language providing that the authorization may be made on the same document as the disclosure."
  — Syed v. M-I, LLC, 853 F.3d 492 (9th Cir. 2017) (https://www.courtlistener.com/opinion/4340133/sarmad-syed-v-m-i-llc/)
  Known gap: This authorizes only the specific report described above — a consumer report obtained for employment purposes. It doesn't authorize adding other terms to this document, and it doesn't authorize using the report for any purpose beyond that one; combining unrelated terms into this document is exactly the practice the case cited above held unlawful.

IF THE REPORT LEADS TO A NEGATIVE DECISION
If this report leads Acme, Inc. to consider an adverse decision based on it — not hiring Jordan Lee, or another employment decision — federal law requires two things before that decision is final: Jordan Lee must receive a copy of the report itself, and a written description of consumer rights under this law, before the adverse action is taken.

[Verified — checked 2026-08-29]
  "Except as provided in subparagraph (B), in using a consumer report for employment purposes, before taking any adverse action based in whole or in part on the report, the person intending to take such adverse action shall provide to the consumer to whom the report relates— (i) a copy of the report; and (ii) a description in writing of the rights of the consumer under this subchapter, as prescribed by the Bureau under section 1681g(c)(3) of this title."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)(A) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, pre-adverse-action requirement (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681b)
  "If any person takes any adverse action with respect to any consumer that is based in whole or in part on any information contained in a consumer report, the person shall— (1) provide oral, written, or electronic notice of the adverse action to the consumer; ... (3) provide to the consumer orally, in writing, or electronically— (A) the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency ... that furnished the report to the person; and (B) a statement that the consumer reporting agency did not make the decision to take the adverse action and is unable to provide the consumer the specific reasons why the adverse action was taken; and (4) provide to the consumer an oral, written, or electronic notice of the consumer’s right— (A) to obtain ... a free copy of a consumer report ...; and (B) to dispute ... the accuracy or completeness of any information in a consumer report furnished by the agency."
  — 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a) (Cornell LII text), U.S. Code, Fair Credit Reporting Act, final adverse-action notice (https://www.law.cornell.edu/uscode/text/15/1681m)
  Known gap: The statute doesn't specify a minimum number of days between this pre-adverse-action notice and a final decision — unlike fixed waiting periods that appear elsewhere in federal employment law, this provision requires only that the report and rights description be provided before the adverse action is taken, without stating how long after that a decision may follow. Separately, once a final adverse decision is actually made, a second, different notice is required under a different provision of this same law — covering the reporting agency's contact information and the consumer's right to a free report and to dispute inaccurate information. This document covers only the earlier, pre-decision step described above, not that later notice.

ACKNOWLEDGMENT
Please sign below to indicate your understanding of and agreement to the disclosure and authorization above.

Applicant / Employee: Jordan Lee
Date: _______________
